From leg geometry to C++ control

I want the model and the software to agree about the robot before asking a controller to use them.

My control work includes analytical forward and inverse kinematics, Jacobian calculations, and numerical comparisons. The geometry is separate from actuator signs, offsets, and gearing, so the same leg model can be checked independently of motor hardware.

Damped least-squares mapping
q̇ = (JᵀJ + λ²I)−1 Jᵀvfoot

The damping term λ²I regularizes the Jacobian calculation. The C++ implementation below uses a linear solve to compute the mapping instead of explicitly inverting the matrix.

LegController.cpp · damped Jacobian solveC++ / Eigen
const Eigen::Matrix3d jacobian_transpose =
    forward_jacobian.transpose();
const Eigen::Matrix3d normal_matrix =
    jacobian_transpose * forward_jacobian +
    jacobian_damping * jacobian_damping *
        Eigen::Matrix3d::Identity();
return normal_matrix.ldlt().solve(jacobian_transpose);

Mass properties are part of the model

A CAD export can have the right shape and still omit mass-bearing components. I worked through component accounting, center of mass, inertia orientation, and frame conventions before using the model as a dynamics foundation.

The corrected simulation model has 13 links, 12 moving joints, and 12.54 kg of CAD-derived mass. That number describes this model and component snapshot; it is not a measured weight for every physical robot revision.

Rotate and shift each component inertia
Itotal = Σ [RiIiRiᵀ + mi((di·di)I − didiᵀ)]

Each component inertia is rotated into a common frame, then shifted to the aggregate center of mass with the parallel-axis theorem. The component masses are accounted for directly rather than scaled by a single global factor.

verify_mass_correction.py · inertia aggregationPython / NumPy
axes = b.ximat[index].reshape(3, 3)
delta = b.xipos[index] - center
inertia += axes @ np.diag(new.body_inertia[index]) @ axes.T
inertia += new.body_mass[index] * (
    np.dot(delta, delta) * np.eye(3) - np.outer(delta, delta)
)

A learning pipeline with explicit contracts

The current learning work uses MuJoCo and Python, versioned experiment settings, saved checkpoints, and ONNX policy-export checks. The observation and action definitions are explicit: 83 observations and 36 actions, with position, velocity, and feedforward-torque commands for the twelve joints.

DOCUMENTED PIPELINE CHECKS · OCTOBER 2026

Check the interfaces before evaluating the behavior.

The current validation record reports 57 regression tests, a short training smoke run, and Python-to-ONNX parity checks. These establish useful pipeline checks; successful locomotion requires a separate behavioral evaluation.

Current stage

PROJECT STATUS

The model and pipeline are foundations for further control work.

The smoke policy mostly stands and has not demonstrated learned walking or trotting. Contact behavior, motor limits, drivetrain dynamics, and transfer to powered hardware still need validation. LQR and centroidal MPC remain preliminary study and development work.

This project has taught me to ask two different questions: does the software execute consistently, and does the model reproduce the behavior I need?
